frontmatter.title: 4. Electroacoustics
frontmatter.subtitle: How sound is captured, processed, digitised, and reproduced through technology

children.value: is the branch of acoustics concerned with converting sound into electrical signals and back again, through devices such as microphones, loudspeakers, and amplifiers. It underpins nearly all modern music making, recording, and reproduction, and it is where the
; every choice in a microphone or converter (sample rate, bit depth, codec) decides what survives that crossing.

The field of electroacoustics began in the late nineteenth century. Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone (1876) showed that speech could be turned into an electrical signal and sent down a wire. Thomas Edison’s phonograph (1877) showed that sound could be recorded and played back mechanically. The carbon microphone, the vacuum tube amplifier, and the moving-coil loudspeaker, all developed in the early twentieth century, made electrical sound reproduction practical.
gives a short account of how these developments reshaped music.

The condenser microphone arrived in the 1920s. Magnetic recording, FM radio, and high-fidelity audio in the mid-twentieth century then transformed music production and broadcasting. Today the field keeps changing through digital signal processing, microelectronics, and wireless transmission.
Electroacoustics is a subdiscipline of acoustics, alongside the room and instrument acoustics we met in
. The physics of sound propagation is the same, but electroacoustics adds electrical and electronic phenomena that shape how sound is captured, modified, transmitted, and reproduced.

Every recorded piece of music has passed through microphones, amplifiers, and loudspeakers, and the character of those devices shapes the timbre we hear. Live performance leans on the same equipment. In concert halls and clubs, the choice and placement of microphones and speakers decides how a performance reaches the audience. And electroacoustic instruments, from electric guitars to synthesisers, all involve electroacoustic transduction somewhere in the signal chain.

is any device that converts energy from one form to another. In electroacoustics, we care mainly about devices that convert between acoustic energy (pressure waves in air) and electrical energy (varying voltages or currents).

The key transducers in this chain are the microphone (acoustic → electrical) and the loudspeaker (electrical → acoustic). The intermediate stages (preamplifier, signal processing, power amplifier) operate entirely in the electrical domain.
Different electroacoustic transducers exploit different physical phenomena to convert energy:
: a conductor moving in a magnetic field generates an electrical current (used in dynamic microphones and moving-coil loudspeakers).
: changes in the distance between two charged plates alter the capacitance and produce a voltage (used in condenser microphones and electrostatic loudspeakers).
: certain crystals and ceramics generate an electrical charge when mechanically deformed (used in contact microphones and some transducers).
These all have trade-offs between frequency response, sensitivity, dynamic range, and cost.

is a transducer that converts acoustic pressure variations in the surrounding air into a corresponding electrical signal. The type, quality, and placement of a microphone strongly shape the character of any recording or live sound system.
is the most widely used type in live sound. Its operating principle is electromagnetic induction:
Sound waves cause a thin diaphragm to vibrate.
A voice coil attached to the diaphragm moves within the field of a permanent magnet.
This movement induces an electrical current in the coil, proportional to the velocity of the diaphragm.
Advantages: robust, tolerant of high sound pressure levels, requires no external power supply, relatively inexpensive.
Disadvantages: limited high-frequency response due to the inertia of the diaphragm and coil assembly; generally lower sensitivity than condenser microphones.
Typical examples include the Shure SM58 (vocal microphone) and Shure SM57 (instrument microphone), which are industry standards in live sound.
Figure: The Shure SM58, a classic dynamic stage microphone (photo: Iain Fergusson,
The diaphragm forms one plate of a capacitor, with a fixed backplate as the other.
The capacitor is maintained at a fixed charge (either by a battery or by phantom power supplied through the microphone cable).
Sound waves cause the diaphragm to move, varying the distance between the plates and hence the capacitance.
This change in capacitance at constant charge produces a varying voltage, which is the output signal.
Advantages: very flat and extended frequency response, high sensitivity, low self-noise, available in small diaphragm (pencil) and large diaphragm varieties.
Disadvantages: requires power (phantom power at 48 V, or internal battery); more fragile than dynamic microphones; more expensive.

Condenser microphones are commonly chosen for studio recording of acoustic instruments, voices, and orchestras, because their flat, extended response and low self-noise capture fine detail. Large-diaphragm condensers (e.g., Neumann U87) are a staple of professional studios.
Figure: The Neumann U87, a large-diaphragm condenser studio microphone (photo: PJ,
uses a thin corrugated metallic ribbon suspended in a magnetic field:
Sound waves cause the ribbon to vibrate within the magnetic field.
The movement of the ribbon induces a voltage by electromagnetic induction, similar to a dynamic microphone, but the ribbon itself is both the diaphragm and the conductor.

Advantages: natural and smooth high-frequency roll-off, excellent transient response, often described as having a warm and vintage sound character. Ribbon microphones are inherently bidirectional (figure-8 polar pattern).

Disadvantages: fragile ribbon element; lower output level, requiring a high-gain preamplifier; sensitive to wind and plosive sounds; some classic ribbon microphones should not be connected to phantom power (though modern active ribbon microphones require it).

are semiconductor-based transducers fabricated using integrated circuit manufacturing techniques. They are used in smartphones, laptops, hearing aids, and other consumer devices where small size matters most. Their performance has improved dramatically in recent years, and they are increasingly found in professional measurement applications as well.

(or directivity pattern) describes how sensitive a microphone is to sounds arriving from different directions. It is typically represented as a plot of sensitivity versus angle, in polar coordinates.
: equal sensitivity in all directions. Captures the full acoustic environment, including room reflections.
: most sensitive in front, least sensitive at the rear (heart-shaped pattern). The most common pattern for live sound and studio recording. Offers some rejection of unwanted sounds from behind.

In practice, polar patterns vary with frequency. Most directional microphones are more omnidirectional at low frequencies and become more directional as frequency increases. The plots below illustrate idealised patterns.

is a common phenomenon in directional (cardioid, figure-8) microphones. The bass response increases when the sound source is very close to the microphone (within 30–60 cm). This effect is exploited by vocalists and broadcasters to achieve a richer, fuller sound, but can be a problem when recording at close range if unwanted bass boost is not desired.

    """Logistic-style smooth transition centred on x0."""
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(x - x0) / width))

# Simulate idealised frequency responses (in dB, relative to 1 kHz)

# Dynamic: slight presence peak ~5 kHz, high-frequency roll-off above 12 kHz

    2.5 * np.exp(-((np.log10(freq) - np.log10(5000)) ** 2) / (2 * 0.15 ** 2))
    - 6 * smooth_step(np.log10(freq), np.log10(12000), 0.15)

    - 2 * smooth_step(np.log10(freq), np.log10(18000), 0.1)

The specification sheet is only half the story, though. Engineers do not choose an SM58 or a U87 because one is “better”; they choose a sound. Microphones colour what they capture, and those colours have become part of music history: the crooner’s intimacy is a sensitive microphone up close, and much of what we recognise as the sound of a favourite record is a chain of such choices. Reading a specification sheet tells you what a microphone can do; listening through it tells you what it does to the music.

Look up the specifications of two microphones: one dynamic (e.g., Shure SM58) and one condenser (e.g., Neumann U87). Compare their self-noise, maximum SPL, and frequency response. For what recording situations would each be better suited?
converts electrical signals into acoustic pressure variations. It is the final electroacoustic transducer in most audio reproduction systems.
is by far the most common loudspeaker type. Its operation is the electromagnetic inverse of the dynamic microphone:
An alternating electrical current flows through a voice coil suspended in a permanent magnetic field.
The interaction of the current and the magnetic field produces a force on the coil (Lorentz force), causing it to move back and forth.
The coil is attached to a cone (diaphragm), whose movement creates pressure waves in the surrounding air.
Most practical loudspeaker systems use several drivers, each optimised for a different frequency range:
: handles low frequencies (bass), typically 20–500 Hz. Large diameter cone (15–40 cm) for efficient low-frequency radiation.
: covers middle frequencies (500 Hz – 5 kHz), where much of the energy of speech and music is concentrated.
: handles high frequencies (5–20 kHz). Small diameter diaphragm (2–4 cm) for extended high-frequency response.
: dedicated low-frequency driver (20–200 Hz) for cinema, music production, and concert sound reinforcement.
routes the appropriate frequencies to each driver, ensuring that each operates within its optimal range.

A high electrical field is maintained between the stators and the diaphragm; applying an audio signal to the stators causes the diaphragm to vibrate. Electrostatic loudspeakers are valued for their extremely low distortion and transient accuracy, but are expensive, large, and require high-voltage power supplies.

Most headphones use dynamic (moving-coil) drivers; high-end models may use planar magnetic or electrostatic elements. The acoustics of headphones differ fundamentally from loudspeakers in a room, since headphones bypass the effects of room acoustics and the pinnae, which can affect perceived spatial image. This makes them attractive for controlled listening experiments in music psychology research, but means that recordings mixed on headphones may translate differently to loudspeakers.

Headphone listening also deserves a moment of reflection. For most people today, most music arrives through earbuds. This is a private, portable listening situation that is completely differnt than how music has been experienced throughout human history. The sound appears inside the head rather than at a place in the room, nobody around you knows what you are hearing, and the music travels with you in changing environments and contexts. This creates a very different listening experience than when playing, listening, moving (including dancing) together. This is important to reflecton on when we study music and its effects.
How do you usually listen to music? How does it influence your experience?

Like microphones, loudspeakers are characterised by their frequency response. Unlike microphones, achieving a flat frequency response across the full audio range from a single transducer is very difficult, which is why multi-driver systems with crossovers are standard.

of a loudspeaker is typically specified as the sound pressure level (in dB SPL) produced at a distance of 1 metre when driven with 1 watt (or 2.83 V into an 8 Ω load). A loudspeaker with higher sensitivity requires less amplifier power to achieve a given sound pressure level.

def bandpass_response(f, f_low, f_high, slope_low=24, slope_high=24):
    """Simulate a bandpass driver response with gentle Butterworth-like slopes."""
    low_shelf  = 1 / np.sqrt(1 + (f_low / f) ** slope_low)
    high_shelf = 1 / np.sqrt(1 + (f / f_high) ** slope_high)
    return 20 * np.log10(low_shelf * high_shelf + 1e-10)

A loudspeaker does not operate in isolation, it interacts strongly with the room in which it is placed. Reflections from walls, floor, and ceiling combine with the direct sound at the listener’s ears, modifying the perceived frequency response and spatial character.

That is not true; you can easily test this by moving a subwoofer around in a room. Try to place it in a corner, then 1 meter from a wall and in the middle of the room. This will change the experienced bass sound more than any equaliser will.
A speaker close to a wall radiates more low end, because the reflection reinforces the direct sound; a corner adds more still. This is
, and it is why the same speaker sounds different once you move it.

When setting up two speakers in a stereo setup, the usual starting point is an equilateral triangle: you at one corner, the two speakers at the others tilted towards you so that the tweeters are at ear height and away from walls.

These effects mean that the same loudspeaker can sound quite different in different rooms, and that acoustic treatment of the room and careful speaker placement are as important as the choice of loudspeaker itself.

is a device that increases the power, voltage, or current of an electrical signal. In an audio signal chain, amplification is necessary because microphones produce very small voltages (millivolts) while loudspeakers require much larger voltages and currents to produce audible sound.
Audio signals travel at very different strengths at various points in the signal chain, and equipment expects a particular one at each input. From weakest to strongest:
(needs a preamplifier before anything else can use it),

(the amplified signal driving a passive loudspeaker). Plugging a signal into an input expecting a different level is the single most common cause of a recording that is either buried in noise or badly distorted.

(preamp) amplifies a microphone-level signal to line level. A high-quality microphone preamplifier is essential for maintaining a low noise floor. Many modern audio interfaces for recording contain built-in microphone preamplifiers. Professional recording studios may use high-quality external preamps (e.g., API 312, Neve 1073) that contribute to the characteristic sound of recordings made in those facilities.

Modern Class D amplifiers (switching amplifiers) are efficient enough (>80%) to run on batteries without much heat.
Most condenser microphones require an external power source to maintain the charge on the capacitor element.

(standardised at 48 V DC, denoted +48V) is supplied through the microphone cable by the preamplifier or audio interface. It is called ‘phantom’ because it does not interfere with the audio signal, which travels as a differential (balanced) pair on the same conductors. Dynamic and ribbon microphones generally do not require phantom power (and some older ribbon microphones can be damaged by it).

A balanced connection carries the audio signal twice: once as a normal-polarity signal and once with the polarity inverted. is the practice of setting appropriate signal levels at each stage of the signal chain to maximise signal-to-noise ratio while avoiding clipping (distortion from exceeding the maximum signal level). Each stage should receive a signal that is neither so weak that noise becomes significant, nor so strong that it clips. In digital audio systems, clipping above 0 dBFS (decibels relative to full scale) causes severe digital distortion.

Signal processing is the field concerned with analysing, modifying, and synthesising signals such as sound, images, and scientific measurements. In electroacoustics and audio engineering, it is how we improve sound quality, pull out information, and adapt audio for specific uses.

Signal processing can happen in both the analogue and the digital domain. The important thing to remember is that everything you hear through a loudspeaker is processed, either manually or (increasingly) automatically: filtering and equalisation shape the tone, compression evens out the dynamics, and reverberation and other effects place the sound in a real or imagined space. The same operations run in a guitar pedal, a mixing console, a phone, and a hearing aid.
Dig deeper: main uses of signal processing in audio
: increasing the strength of electrical signals so they can drive loudspeakers or be recorded at usable levels.
: removing unwanted frequencies (such as noise or hum) or enhancing desired frequency ranges. Filters can be low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or notch filters.
: adjusting the balance between frequency components to shape the tonal quality of audio signals.
: reducing the difference between the loudest and quietest parts of a signal to make audio more consistent and prevent distortion.
: techniques such as gating, spectral subtraction, or adaptive filtering to minimise background noise.
: adding reverberation, delay, chorus, distortion, or other effects to enhance or creatively alter the sound.
: changing aspects of the signal such as amplitude, frequency, or phase for transmission or synthesis.

: a circuit or algorithm that produces a repeating waveform at a chosen frequency. Four waveforms dominate, and each has its own spectrum and therefore its own timbre. A sine wave contains only its fundamental and sounds pure, like the deep sub-bass under much hip-hop. The triangle wave adds weak odd harmonics and sounds soft and flute-like. The square wave has strong odd harmonics and a hollow, reedy character familiar from chiptune game music. The sawtooth wave contains every harmonic and sounds bright and buzzy, which makes it the usual starting point for rich lead and string sounds.

The sampling rate is the number of samples per second taken from a continuous signal to create a discrete signal. According to the
, the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal to reconstruct it accurately. This minimum limit is known as the
. Since humans can hear frequencies up to around 20,000 Hz, this means that sound needs to be sampled at more than 40,000 Hz to capture all audible sound.

Digital audio has for a long time been standardised at using 44,100 Hz, which can represent frequencies up to 22,050 Hz. The oddly specific number is a piece of history dating back to the introduction of the CD. The rate had to be a little above twice the 20 kHz upper limit of hearing, to leave room for the anti-aliasing filter that removes everything above the Nyquist frequency before sampling. The exact value came from video. In the late 1970s the only recorders with enough bandwidth for digital audio were video tape machines, so early systems such as Sony’s PCM adaptors stored the audio samples as a pseudo-video picture, three samples per television line. 44,100 Hz is the rate that fits a whole number of samples into both television standards: 60 fields per second × 245 usable lines × 3 samples in NTSC, and 50 × 294 × 3 in PAL, both give 44,100. When Sony and Philips finalised the CD in 1980, the mastering recorders already ran at this rate, and it has stayed with us ever since. Professional recording often uses 48 kHz, 96 kHz, or higher. Higher sampling rates can reduce aliasing, where frequencies too high to be represented reappear as false lower tones (demonstrated below), and leave more headroom for some processing tasks, but they also increase file size and CPU load.

is the amount of data used to represent each individual sample in a digital audio signal. Bit depth sets the precision of the stored amplitude values: higher bit depths give lower quantisation noise and a greater dynamic range. CDs use 16 bits per sample, professional recording usually 24, and modern recorders increasingly 32-bit floating point, whose enormous headroom means that even a badly set recording level can often be rescued afterwards. At normal listening levels the audible differences are small; what the extra bits buy is safety margin while recording and processing.
If you had to choose, would you prefer to have a higher sampling rate (e.g. 96 kHz and 16-bit) or a higher bit rate (e.g. 44.1 kHz and 32-bit)?

In a digital audio workstation (DAW), a live performance setup, or a real-time synthesis patch, audio is processed in
(buffers) of samples rather than as one infinite stream. The buffer size, together with the sampling rate, sets how often the computer must finish a round of processing. A smaller buffer means lower

, the delay between input and output, but it leaves less time per block and raises CPU load. A larger buffer is more forgiving with heavy plug-ins, but it increases latency and can make timing feel sluggish when you monitor yourself or play virtual instruments.

Round-trip latency comes from several places: analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue conversion, buffering in the driver and the application, and the digital signal processing in the chain. Interfaces and drivers often report separate input and output figures, but what matters to a performer is the total monitoring delay. To avoid hearing themselves late, many systems offer direct monitoring, an analogue path from input to headphones that bypasses the computer.

At the University of Oslo, we have been researching network music performance for many years. This is based on the musicians being in different locations, which, by design, introduces latency. There are many technological challenges in making this work in practice. There are also many interesting psychological lessons to be learned from such experimentation. Finally, it can also lead to interesting musical results.

How does a lossy codec decide what to remove? This is where electroacoustics leans directly on
splits the signal into frequency bands and, moment by moment, runs a psychoacoustic model of what a human ear would actually notice. The key phenomenon is

: a strong sound makes weaker sounds close to it in frequency (simultaneous masking) or in time (temporal masking) inaudible. Components the model predicts are masked can be stored very coarsely or discarded altogether, and the saved bits are spent where hearing is most sensitive.

This is why an MP3 file at a typical streaming bitrate keeps less than a tenth of the data in the CD-quality original, yet most listeners cannot tell the difference. Push the bitrate lower and the model must start discarding components that are not fully masked, which is when the familiar artefacts appear: a swirly, underwater quality, most audible in cymbals, reverb tails, and other noise-like sounds. Lossy compression is, in other words, applied psychoacoustics: a working monument to the fact that we do not hear everything that reaches our ears.

The ears locate a sound using three cues: the difference in arrival time between the ears, the difference in level, and the filtering the head and outer ear impose. How these cues work in perception is explained in the next chapter,
. Spatial audio is the engineering side of the same problem. Given loudspeakers or headphones, how do you deliver those cues convincingly?

The oldest and still the most common approach stores one signal per loudspeaker. Stereo is the familiar case. A source panned between two speakers is not really located anywhere: sending the same signal to both at equal level produces a

, which the listener hears as coming from a point between the speakers even though nothing is radiating from there. Adjusting the balance slides the image left or right. Surround formats such as 5.1 extend the idea with more speakers, adding rear channels for ambience and a dedicated low-frequency channel.
Channel-based audio is simple and robust, but the mix is made for one specific loudspeaker layout, and the illusion is only reliable in the
, the small region roughly equidistant from the speakers. If you move off-centre, the phantom images collapse towards whichever speaker you are nearest.
If the spatial cues are things that happen at the two eardrums, then delivering them over headphones is a matter of reproducing the right signal at each ear. That is what

Binaural audio can be convincing, but it has two well-known problems. HRTFs are individual, since they depend on the shape of your head, torso, and outer ears, so a generic HRTF localises less well for most listeners, but not all. Also, a static binaural rendering turns with your head, which the real world does not do. That is why many virtual reality (VR) systems use head trackers to rotate the auditory scene to compensate.

The third approach stores neither speakers nor ears, but a description of the sound field itself, which is then decoded to whatever the playback system happens to be.

is the main example: a full-sphere surround technique whose first-order recordings carry four channels, together known as B-format, that capture both the overall sound pressure at a point and which direction the sound is coming from. Higher orders add further channels, sharpening the spatial resolution at the cost of more of them.

The practical appeal is that recording and reproduction are decoupled. One ambisonic recording can be decoded to a pair of headphones, to a stereo pair, or to a dome of thirty speakers, and it can be rotated before decoding, which is what makes it the usual carrier format for virtual reality and 360-degree video. Because such a recording stores direction as well as level, it can also be analysed to reveal where sound comes from and how diffuse it is;
puts this to use for describing everyday sound environments.

A fourth approach, common in cinema, stores each source as a mono signal plus metadata saying where it should be, and leaves the renderer in the playback room to work out which speakers to use. This is object-based audio, and it is best understood as deferring the panning decision from the mixing stage to the listening stage.

is the best-known example. It began in cinemas in 2012, where a mix of up to 128 objects is rendered to whatever speaker array the theatre has, including overhead speakers for height. Since the early 2020s it has also become a delivery format for music: streaming services offer Atmos mixes of albums, and on headphones these are rendered binaurally, so most listeners meet object-based audio as a form of binaural playback.

Atmos and ambisonics are easy to confuse, since both promise independence from the playback layout, but they store different things. An ambisonic recording describes the sound field at one point, sources and room together, and the decoder derives speaker or headphone feeds from that description; it can be captured directly with a microphone and rotated as a whole. Atmos stores individual sources, each a mono signal with metadata about where it should be, and the renderer places them on whatever speakers exist. That makes it a production format rather than a recording format: objects are authored in a mix, and a room cannot be recorded into Atmos the way it can with an ambisonic microphone. In practice the two often meet, as when a game or VR engine carries the ambience as ambisonics and the characters as objects, and both end up rendered binaurally on headphones.

children.value: Streaming services sell tiers of sound quality, and hi-fi magazines have argued for decades that 24-bit audio at 96 or 192 kHz sounds audibly better than the 16-bit, 44.1 kHz standard of the CD. The chapter has explained what those numbers mean, which makes this a good claim to test against listening experiments.

cuts both ways. In one widely cited study, a CD-quality analogue-to-digital-to-analogue loop was inserted into the playback of high-resolution recordings on high-end systems, and over more than five hundred blind trials the listeners, many of them audiophiles and audio professionals, picked the right one about half the time, which is chance

. A later meta-analysis pooled eighteen studies with over twelve thousand trials and found a small but statistically reliable ability to tell the formats apart, a few percentage points above chance overall and clearer for listeners who had been trained on the task

in both cases is blind discrimination: the listener hears two versions and must say whether they differ, without knowing which is which. The disagreement is partly about material. Critics of the first study argued that many of its recordings had been mastered from 44.1 or 48 kHz sources and so contained nothing to hear; critics of the meta-analysis note that it pools studies with very different designs.

are the important part. Where a difference is found, it is tiny, it needs training to detect, and detecting a difference is not the same as preferring it. Mastering choices, loudspeakers, and the room change the sound far more than the format does.

The chapter’s account of sampling explains why. A 44.1 kHz rate already captures the audible range, and 16 bits with dither put the quantisation noise below the noise of any listening room. The real value of higher rates and depths lies in production, where headroom and processing margin matter. Recording at 24 bits is sound engineering; paying to stream at 192 kHz is mostly buying a number.

Electroacoustics follows sound from the air into a wire and back again. Microphones and loudspeakers are the transducers at either end, and preamplifiers, converters, processors, and power amplifiers work in the electrical domain between them. Each microphone type (dynamic, condenser, ribbon, MEMS) trades robustness, sensitivity, and self-noise differently, and its polar pattern and frequency response colour what it captures, which is why engineers choose a sound rather than a specification. Loudspeakers and headphones do the reverse job, and where they sit, in a room or in the ears, shapes the result as much as the device itself. Signal levels and gain staging keep the chain clean, balanced connections keep it quiet, and processing (filtering, equalisation, compression, effects) touches everything we hear. Synthesisers generate the signal from scratch, whether by subtracting from rich waveforms, adding partials, modulating frequencies, or replaying and reshaping recorded sound. Digital audio adds sampling and quantisation, whose rate and bit depth decide what survives the crossing into numbers, with latency, perceptual codecs, and file formats as the practical consequences. Spatial audio delivers the localisation cues over loudspeakers (channel-based), headphones (binaural), a description of the sound field (ambisonics), or sources with position metadata (object-based formats such as Atmos). Running underneath the technology are two reflective threads: recorded sound is split from its source (schizophonia), and every device in the chain, from the choice of microphone to the earbuds most music is now heard through, colours the music rather than neutrally transmitting it. A critical look at high-resolution audio showed that blind listening tests find at most a tiny, trained difference from CD quality, and that the extra bits earn their keep in production rather than playback.
